input.transcript:
User: What did Northern Alliance leaders agree on defence spending, and who objected?

Assistant: Northern Alliance leaders agreed to a joint defence spending goal of 5 percent of national output by 2035, which is divided into 3.5 percent for core defence and 1.5 percent for related spending such as resilience and cyber defence [Northern Alliance leaders adopt 5% spending goal](https://news.example/2026/06/alliance-summit-spending-target). However, Norland's prime minister objected to this target, calling it unrealistic for her country's economy and stating that it would lead to cuts in pensions rather than military spending. She mentioned that Norland's current spending level of 2.1 percent is sufficient and claimed that an exemption for members facing budget constraints was informally agreed upon, although this was not reflected in the official communiqué [Norland says 5% target is unrealistic](https://news.example/2026/06/norland-rejects-spending-target).

In contrast, Vestria supported the 5 percent target but disputed Norland's claim of an exemption, emphasizing that the communiqué is the complete agreement without any opt-out clause. Vestria's delegation also sought a broader definition of related spending to include infrastructure that supports defence readiness [Vestria backs target, asks for flexibility](https://news.example/2026/06/vestria-backs-target-with-caveats).

outline: Spending breakdown: 3.5% core defence and 1.5% related spending
Norland's objections: feasibility, pension impact, 2.1% current spending, claimed exemption
Vestria's response: supports target, disputes exemption, seeks broader related-spending definition (infrastructure)

# Northern Alliance defence-spending outcome and member reactions

## 1. 5% defence-spending target agreed (by 2035)
Northern Alliance leaders agreed to a joint defence spending goal of 5 percent of national output to be reached by 2035. This agreement was described as a collective target at the summit [Northern Alliance leaders adopt 5% spending goal](https://news.example/2026/06/alliance-summit-spending-target).

The transcript indicates there was immediate pushback from at least one member (see Section 3), but provides no further detail in this section on enforcement mechanisms, timetables for interim milestones, monitoring arrangements, or consequences for non-compliance. Those implementation details are not present in the supplied text.

## 2. Spending breakdown: 3.5% core defence and 1.5% related spending
The 5 percent target is presented as a split between 3.5 percent for core defence spending and 1.5 percent for related spending. The related spending category was illustrated in the transcript with examples such as resilience and cyber defence [Northern Alliance leaders adopt 5% spending goal](https://news.example/2026/06/alliance-summit-spending-target).

The transcript does not provide a formal, detailed definition of what counts as "related spending" beyond the examples given, nor does it set out accounting rules, verification standards, or which specific programme lines should be reclassified. Those definitional and accounting questions are not answered in the supplied text.

## 3. Norland's objections: feasibility, pension impact, 2.1% current spending, claimed exemption
Norland's prime minister objected to the 5 percent target, describing it as unrealistic for her country's economy and warning that meeting it would result in cuts to pensions rather than to civilian programmes opposed to military spending. She stated that Norland's current defence spending stands at 2.1 percent and contended that an exemption for members facing budget constraints had been informally agreed, although that exemption does not appear in the official communiqué [Norland says 5% target is unrealistic](https://news.example/2026/06/norland-rejects-spending-target).

The transcript does not supply supporting economic data from Norland (for example, fiscal projections, pension budget figures, or simulations showing how the increase would be financed), nor does it provide the text of any informal exemption or describe how such an exemption would have been agreed. Those substantive evidentiary details are absent from the supplied material.

## 4. Vestria's response: supports target, disputes exemption, seeks broader related-spending definition (infrastructure)
Vestria publicly supported the 5 percent target and disputed Norland's claim that an exemption had been agreed. Vestria emphasized that the communiqué represents the complete agreement and that there is no opt-out clause recorded. Vestria's delegation also sought a broader definition of related spending to explicitly include infrastructure that supports defence readiness [Vestria backs target, asks for flexibility](https://news.example/2026/06/vestria-backs-target-with-caveats).

The transcript does not provide details on which specific infrastructure items Vestria proposes to count as related spending, nor does it include whether other members accepted or rejected that broader definition. Those specific positions and any vote or consensus text on definitional scope are not present in the supplied text.
